# Comparing Groups as Regression

Last week ended with a magic trick: you ran a t-test, then ran the same question through `lm()`, and the numbers matched exactly. This week we pull the trick apart and show you the wires.

The key move is **dummy coding** — the trick that lets a model with only numbers in it handle a variable like "treatment group." Once you see it, two things happen. First, the t-test stops being a separate procedure and becomes a regression with one categorical predictor. Second, **ANOVA** does too: three groups is just two dummy variables instead of one.

We will also deal with the question that comes up the moment you have three groups: why not just run a t-test on every pair? (Short answer: because your false-positive rate quietly climbs to 14%.)

::: callout-note
## A small thing that matters a lot

Software picks the reference group alphabetically. Your research question almost never does. Choosing the reference group deliberately is one of the easiest ways to make a results table say what you actually mean.
:::
